title: Data Locality
explain: Moving a task to the data is usually cheaper than moving the data to the task. Data locality means scheduling work on the machine that already holds, or just produced, its inputs. In my scheduler design a worker announces what it holds when it asks for work, and the dispatcher counts locality as one factor in the score.
model:
A task has inputs `[D1, D2, ...]` and outputs `[D3, D5, ...]`. A worker that has just finished a task now *holds* D3 and D5.

```
worker: "give me work. I have D3, D5."
dispatcher: scores pending tasks
   +locality match (task needs D3, D5)   <- can start instantly, no transfer
   -load on this worker
   +priority / fairness
   -> assign best; if no good match, wait a bounded time, then hand over a non-local task
```

- **Worker-reported placement:** the worker's own report is the current truth (including evictions), so the dispatcher needs no global location catalogue that can drift.
- **Delay scheduling:** a short, *bounded* wait often lets a local task appear; an unbounded wait idles workers and starves tasks.
- **A preference, not a rule:** balance against load so a popular dataset does not funnel every task to one worker; replicate hot data.

Same idea at many levels: CPU caches, disk pages, a [JSONB document](#/sd/f/json-vs-sql) holding what one read needs, and LLM requests routed to the replica holding the [prefix cache](#/sd/f/load-balancing). The scheduler role is the [dispatcher](#/sd/f/dispatcher).

details.q: A worker asks for work and no pending task uses its data, but one probably will soon. What should the dispatcher do?
details.a: Make it wait a bounded time for a local match, then give it any task. A bounded wait gains locality when it is likely and costs at most the bound when not; waiting forever starves tasks, never waiting pays the transfer every time.

details.q: How do you size the wait? Take 6 GB of input at 125 MB/s and 20 s of compute.
details.a: Running remotely now costs 6,000 MB / 125 MB/s = 48 s transfer + 20 s compute = 68 s. Waiting W seconds for a local worker costs W + 20, so the break-even is 48 s. Set the bound well below that to allow for uncertainty.

details.q: What goes wrong if the dispatcher scores purely by locality?
details.a: A popular dataset's worker becomes a hotspot while others idle, for example 5,000 tasks on D9. Combine locality with load or queue depth and priority, and replicate hot data to more workers.

details.q: Why have the worker announce "I have D3, D5" instead of keeping a central map?
details.a: The worker is the authoritative, current source on what it holds, including after evictions. A central map must be kept in sync, and any lag sends tasks to workers that no longer have the data.

details.q: Where else does data locality show up?
details.a: CPU caches and disk pages, pipeline stages consuming the previous stage's output, a document row that holds everything one read needs, and routing LLM requests to the replica already holding the prompt's prefix cache.

details.q: What are the downsides of locality-aware scheduling?
details.a: More dispatcher complexity, a risk of load skew, and stale or evicted data causing mismatches. Treat locality as a score term and measure the transfer it saves.

prompts.q: Explain data locality in a task scheduler with the "I have D3, D5" flow.
points: Run the task where its inputs already are
Worker reports the data it holds when asking for work
Dispatcher scores tasks including a locality-match term
No perfect match leads to a bounded wait, then a non-local task

prompts.q: Why must the wait for a local task be bounded, and how do you choose the bound?
points: Unbounded waiting idles workers and starves tasks
Compare transfer cost with the wait
Break-even wait equals the transfer time
Choose a bound well below that, given uncertainty

prompts.q: Describe how to keep a locality-aware scheduler from creating hotspots.
points: Locality is one score term, not a rule
Include load or queue depth and priority
Fall back to non-local when the local worker is busy
